claim: The study analyzed 105 research participants, including 73 COVID19 patients versus 32 negative controls.
source: In order to investigate variations in the pathophysiological state of COVID19 patients, we completed an integrated analysis of 105 research participants, including 73 COVID19 patients versus 32 negative controls (Figure 1a).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of participants and their COVID19 status in the methods description.

claim: COVID19 patients tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 infection by PCR and/or antibody testing and were hospitalized due to COVID19 symptoms.
source: COVID19 patients tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 infection by PCR and/or antibody testing and were hospitalized due to COVID19 symptoms, but none of them had developed severe pathology requiring ICU admission at the time of blood collection.
evidence: The manuscript describes the inclusion criteria for COVID19 patients in the study cohort.

claim: None of the COVID19 patients had developed severe pathology requiring ICU admission at the time of blood collection.
source: COVID19 patients tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 infection by PCR and/or antibody testing and were hospitalized due to COVID19 symptoms, but none of them had developed severe pathology requiring ICU admission at the time of blood collection.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the disease severity status of the COVID19 cohort.

claim: The COVID19 cohort displayed significantly elevated levels of anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgGs in all four assays, with strong inter-individual variability.
source: The COVID19 cohort displayed significantly elevated levels of anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgGs in all four assays, with strong inter-individual variability (Figure 1b).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured antibody levels with reference to Figure 1b showing the data.

claim: Levels of antibodies against the Flu A Hong Kong H3 virus strain were no higher in COVID19 patients.
source: As a control, levels of antibodies against the Flu A Hong Kong H3 virus strain were no higher in COVID19 patients (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The manuscript reports control antibody measurements with reference to supplementary figure data.

claim: In COVID19 patients, reactivity against the spike protein correlated positively with reactivity against the other three peptides.
source: In COVID19 patients, reactivity against the spike protein correlated positively with reactivity against the other three peptides (Figure 1c).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results with reference to Figure 1c.

claim: Top positive correlations among 407 abundant plasma proteins detected by MS are dominated by specific immunoglobulin sequences.
source: Reassuringly, top positive correlations among 407 abundant plasma proteins detected by MS are dominated by specific immunoglobulin sequences, including several that were previously observed to be enriched in the bloodstream of COVID19 patients during seroconversion (Supplementary file 2, Figure 1e–f; Nielsen et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript reports MS proteomics findings with citation to prior work and reference to figures.

claim: Several immunoglobulin sequences were previously observed to be enriched in the bloodstream of COVID19 patients during seroconversion.
source: Reassuringly, top positive correlations among 407 abundant plasma proteins detected by MS are dominated by specific immunoglobulin sequences, including several that were previously observed to be enriched in the bloodstream of COVID19 patients during seroconversion (Supplementary file 2, Figure 1e–f; Nielsen et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work (Nielsen et al., 2020) supporting this observation.

claim: Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) were only mildly elevated in sero-low COVID19 patients relative to the control group but significantly decreased in the circulation of sero-high patients.
source: pDCs were only mildly elevated in sero-low COVID19 patients relative to the control group but significantly decreased in the circulation of sero-high patients (Figure 2c).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured cell frequencies with reference to Figure 2c.

claim: pDCs are predicted to be activated and extravasate into the circulation early on as part of the innate immune response, ahead of development of humoral immunity.
source: Being first responders during a viral infection, pDCs are predicted to be activated and extravasate into the circulation early on as part of the innate immune response, ahead of development of humoral immunity.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation based on established knowledge of pDC function during viral infections.

claim: The significant reduction of pDCs in the bloodstream of sero-high patients could be indicative of exhaustion and/or depletion over the course of the disease.
source: Their significant reduction in the bloodstream of sero-high patients could be indicative of exhaustion and/or depletion over the course of the disease.
evidence: The manuscript provides a speculative interpretation of the observed pDC depletion.

claim: Among CD4+ T cells, elevated frequencies of Th1, Th17, Th1/17, follicular helper CD4+ T cells (TFH), and terminally differentiated effector memory CD45RA+ subsets were observed in sero-low COVID19 patients, with frequencies falling back to baseline or below baseline in sero-high patients.
source: Among CD4+ T cells, we observed elevated frequencies of Th1, Th17, Th1/17, follicular helper CD4+ T cells (TFH), and terminally differentiated effector memory CD45RA+ subsets in sero-low COVID19 patients, with frequencies falling back to baseline or below baseline in sero-high patients (Figure 2a,c).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured T cell subset frequencies with reference to figures.

claim: Among CD8+ T cells, a similar behavior was observed for activated (CD95+), effector (T-bet+Eomes+), senescent (T-bet+ Eomes−), effector memory, and terminally differentiated CD45RA+ subsets.
source: Among CD8+ T cells, a similar behavior was observed for activated (CD95+), effector (T-bet+Eomes+), senescent (T-bet+ Eomes−), effector memory, and terminally differentiated CD45RA+ subsets (Figure 2a–c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured CD8+ T cell subset frequencies with reference to figures.

claim: CD3+ CD4- CD8- T cells (DN T cells) increased only in sero-low patients.
source: Notably, we also observed increases in CD3+ CD4- CD8- T cells (DN T cells) only in sero-low patients (Figure 2a).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured DN T cell frequencies with reference to Figure 2a.

claim: DN T cells display distinct effector phenotypes, including an upregulated cytolytic machinery, and may mediate tissue damage in autoinflammatory conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus and Sjogren's syndrome.
source: DN T cells display distinct effector phenotypes, including an upregulated cytolytic machinery, and may mediate tissue damage in autoinflammatory conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus and Sjogren's syndrome (Brandt and Hedrich, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Brandt and Hedrich, 2018) describing DN T cell characteristics.

claim: CD56bright NK cells increased only in sero-low patients.
source: This bimodal T cell behavior is accompanied by increases in the frequency of CD56bright NK cells only in sero-low patients (Figure 2a,c).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured NK cell frequencies with reference to figures.

claim: CD56bright NK cells lack expression of inhibitory receptors and express high levels of activating receptors, cytokine and chemokine receptors, and adhesion molecules.
source: CD56bright NK cells lack expression of inhibitory receptors and express high levels of activating receptors, cytokine and chemokine receptors, and adhesion molecules (Poli et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Poli et al., 2009) describing CD56bright NK cell characteristics.

claim: CD56bright NK cells are not as cytotoxic as other NK subsets, but they are strong producers of key cytokines involved in the immune response, most prominently IFNG.
source: Although CD56bright NK cells are not as cytotoxic as other NK subsets, they are strong producers of key cytokines involved in the immune response, most prominently IFNG, which we found to be elevated in sero-low patients (see later, Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about CD56bright NK cells and references their own data on IFNG.

claim: IFNG was found to be elevated in sero-low patients.
source: Although CD56bright NK cells are not as cytotoxic as other NK subsets, they are strong producers of key cytokines involved in the immune response, most prominently IFNG, which we found to be elevated in sero-low patients (see later, Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured IFNG levels with reference to Figure 3.

claim: CD56bright NK cells have been found to be elevated in some autoimmune conditions and infections.
source: CD56bright NK cells have been found to be elevated in some autoimmune conditions and infections (Poli et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Poli et al., 2009) describing CD56bright NK cell behavior in disease.

claim: The frequency of total B cells and plasmablasts among CD45+ live cells increased with seroconversion.
source: Somewhat expectedly, the frequency of total B cells and plasmablasts among CD45+ live cells increased with seroconversion (Figure 2a–c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured B cell frequencies with reference to figures.

claim: B cell subsets displaying significant positive association with seroconversion include switched Memory B cells (Switched Bmem), IgM+ memory B cells (IgM+ Bmem), c-delta switched memory B cells (c-delta switched B-mem), and pre-switched activated memory B cells (pre-switched activated Bmem).
source: Other B cell subsets displaying significant positive association with seroconversion include key memory subsets such as switched Memory B cells (Switched Bmem), IgM+ memory B cells (IgM+ Bmem), c-delta switched memory B cells (c-delta switched B-mem), and pre-switched activated memory B cells (pre-switched activated Bmem) (Figure 2a–c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured B cell subset frequencies with reference to figures.

claim: Other B cell subsets enriched in sero-high COVID19 patients include mature naïve B cells and age-dependent B cells (ABCs).
source: Other B cell subsets enriched in sero-high COVID19 patients include mature naïve B cells and age-dependent B cells (ABCs) (Figure 2a,b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured B cell subset frequencies with reference to figures.

claim: An increase in mature naïve B cells is consistent with the development of humoral immunity.
source: An increase in mature naïve B cells is consistent with the development of humoral immunity.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation based on established immunological knowledge.

claim: ABCs are associated with typical aging and development of autoimmunity, but their potential role during viral infections is less understood.
source: ABCs are associated with typical aging and development of autoimmunity, but their potential role during viral infections is less understood (Karnell et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Karnell et al., 2017) describing ABC characteristics.

claim: Among 82 immune factors in the MSD data set, top negative correlations with seroconversion are IFNA2, IFNL1, and IFNG.
source: Among 82 immune factors in the MSD data set, top negative correlations are IFNA2, IFNL1, and IFNG (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b, Figure 3a,b, Supplementary files 4 and 6).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results with reference to figures and supplementary files.

claim: Among 5000+ epitopes measured by SOMAscan, IFNA7, IFNL3, and IFNA1 rank among the top 10 negative correlations with seroconversion.
source: Among 5000+ epitopes measured by SOMAscan, IFNA7, IFNL3, and IFNA1 rank among the top 10 negative correlations with seroconversion (Figure 3a,b, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports SOMAscan correlation analysis results with reference to figures and supplementary files.

claim: All IFN ligands (IFNA2, IFNL1, IFNG, IFNA7, IFNL3, IFNA1) were significantly higher in sero-low COVID19 patients relative to the control cohort, but levels fall back within normal ranges in sero-high COVID19 patients.
source: All these IFN ligands were significantly higher in sero-low COVID19 patients relative to the control cohort, but levels fall back within normal ranges in sero-high COVID19 patients (Figure 3a,c).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured IFN levels with reference to figures.

claim: Elevated plasma levels of key IFN-inducible proteins, such as CXCL10, were observed preferentially in sero-low patients.
source: This notion is further supported by the elevated plasma levels of key IFN-inducible proteins, such as CXCL10 (C-X-C Motif Chemokine Ligand 10, IFN-inducible protein 10, IP10), and elevated expression of IFN-inducible mRNAs (e.g. CXCL10, ISG15, MX1, and IFIT1), preferentially in sero-low patients (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured protein and mRNA levels with reference to figures.

claim: Elevated expression of IFN-inducible mRNAs (e.g. CXCL10, ISG15, MX1, and IFIT1) was observed preferentially in sero-low patients.
source: This notion is further supported by the elevated plasma levels of key IFN-inducible proteins, such as CXCL10 (C-X-C Motif Chemokine Ligand 10, IFN-inducible protein 10, IP10), and elevated expression of IFN-inducible mRNAs (e.g. CXCL10, ISG15, MX1, and IFIT1), preferentially in sero-low patients (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured mRNA expression levels with reference to figures.

claim: This pattern was not evident for IFNB1.
source: Notably, this pattern was not evident for IFNB1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured IFNB1 levels with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Factors involved in monocyte differentiation and activation were preferentially elevated in sero-low patients, such as CCL8, CSF3, and CCL19.
source: Factors involved in monocyte differentiation and activation were also preferentially elevated in sero-low patients, such as CCL8 (C-C Motif Chemokine Ligand 8, Monocyte Chemoattractant Protein 2, MCP2), CSF3 (Colony Stimulating Factor 3, Granulocyte Colony Stimulating Factor, G-CSF), and CCL19 (C-C Motif Chemokine Ligand 19, Macrophage Inflammatory Protein 3 beta, MIP3beta) (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured cytokine levels with reference to figures.

claim: Circulating levels of total monocytes and monocyte subsets are not significantly correlated with seroconversion status.
source: Although circulating levels of total monocytes and monocyte subsets are not significantly correlated with seroconversion status (Supplementary file 5), these results are consistent with a transient round of activation and mobilization of tissue-resident monocytes and macrophages by local IFN production, with subsequent decreases upon seroconversion.
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results with reference to supplementary file.

claim: Circulating levels of CD14 were strongly anticorrelated with seroconversion, being significantly elevated among sero-low patients and significantly depleted in sero-high patients.
source: In support of this notion, we noticed that circulating levels of CD14, a surface marker for monocytes and macrophages, were strongly anticorrelated with seroconversion, being significantly elevated among sero-low patients and significantly depleted in sero-high patients (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured CD14 levels with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: CD14 was the top negative correlation in the MS proteomics dataset.
source: In fact, CD14 was the top negative correlation in the MS proteomics dataset (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results with reference to figures and supplementary files.

claim: Top correlations among immune factors include TNFSF13B and its receptor, TNFRSF17.
source: In agreement with the signs of B cell maturation and differentiation associated with seroconversion (Figure 2a,b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–c), top correlations among immune factors include TNFSF13B (TNF Superfamily Member 13B, B-cell activating factor, BAFF), and its receptor, TNFRSF17 (TNF Receptor Superfamily Member 17, B cell Maturation Protein, BCMA).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results with reference to figures.

claim: TNFSF13B is increased preferentially in sero-low patients relative to the control group.
source: TNFSF13B is increased preferentially in sero-low patients relative to the control group (Figure 3c).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured TNFSF13B levels with reference to Figure 3c.

claim: TNFRSF17 decreases preferentially in sero-low patients, returning to levels similar to the control group upon seroconversion.
source: In contrast, its receptor TNFRSF17 decreases preferentially in sero-low patients, returning to levels similar to the control group upon seroconversion (Figure 3c).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured TNFRSF17 levels with reference to Figure 3c.

claim: The increased levels of TNFSF13B in sero-low patients are consistent with a strong wave of B cell stimulation and proliferation prior to B cell maturation and seroconversion.
source: The increased levels of TNFSF13B in sero-low patients are consistent with a strong wave of B cell stimulation and proliferation prior to B cell maturation and seroconversion.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation based on established knowledge of TNFSF13B function.

claim: The decrease in circulating soluble TNFRSF17 could be interpreted as a consequence of transient lymphopenia prior to seroconversion.
source: The decrease in circulating soluble TNFRSF17 could be interpreted as a consequence of transient lymphopenia prior to seroconversion (see later, Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript provides a speculative interpretation with reference to later data.

claim: Seroconversion associates with a restoration of circulating cytokines depleted preferentially in sero-low COVID19 patients, such as CCL14 and CCL24 (Eotaxin-2).
source: Other interesting top correlations reveal that seroconversion associates with a restoration of circulating cytokines depleted preferentially in sero-low COVID19 patients, such as CCL14 and CCL24 (Eotaxin-2) (Figure 3a).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured cytokine levels with reference to Figure 3a.

claim: Seroconversion is not strongly correlated with changes in acute phase proteins that are commonly elevated upon viral and bacterial infections, such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and ferritin (FTL).
source: Of note, seroconversion is not strongly correlated with changes in acute phase proteins that are commonly elevated upon viral and bacterial infections, such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and ferritin (FTL) (Supplementary files 2–4).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results with reference to supplementary files.

claim: CRP levels measured by MS decrease in sero-high patients.
source: Whereas CRP levels measured by MS decrease in sero-high patients, ferritin levels remain high (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d), suggesting that seroconversion attenuates but does not fully reverse the broader inflammatory phenotype of COVID19.
evidence: The manuscript reports measured CRP levels with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Ferritin levels remain high in sero-high patients.
source: Whereas CRP levels measured by MS decrease in sero-high patients, ferritin levels remain high (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d), suggesting that seroconversion attenuates but does not fully reverse the broader inflammatory phenotype of COVID19.
evidence: The manuscript reports measured ferritin levels with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Seroconversion attenuates but does not fully reverse the broader inflammatory phenotype of COVID19.
source: Whereas CRP levels measured by MS decrease in sero-high patients, ferritin levels remain high (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d), suggesting that seroconversion attenuates but does not fully reverse the broader inflammatory phenotype of COVID19.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation based on the CRP and ferritin data.

claim: IFNA2 levels correlated negatively with key B cell subsets increased upon seroconversion.
source: Indeed, IFNA2 levels correlated negatively with key B cell subsets increased upon seroconversion, and positively with pDCs, T cell subsets decreased upon seroconversion, and CD56bright NK cells (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1e, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results with reference to figures and supplementary files.

claim: IFNA2 levels correlated positively with pDCs, T cell subsets decreased upon seroconversion, and CD56bright NK cells.
source: Indeed, IFNA2 levels correlated negatively with key B cell subsets increased upon seroconversion, and positively with pDCs, T cell subsets decreased upon seroconversion, and CD56bright NK cells (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1e, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results with reference to figures and supplementary files.

claim: 10 of the top 20 negative correlations in the MS data set are complement subunits or complement regulators.
source: In fact, 10 of the top 20 negative correlations in the MS data set are complement subunits or complement regulators, and the top negative correlation in the SOMAscan data set is the complement subunit C1QC (Figure 4a,b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b,c, Supplementary files 2,3).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results with reference to figures and supplementary files.

claim: The top negative correlation in the SOMAscan data set is the complement subunit C1QC.
source: In fact, 10 of the top 20 negative correlations in the MS data set are complement subunits or complement regulators, and the top negative correlation in the SOMAscan data set is the complement subunit C1QC (Figure 4a,b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b,c, Supplementary files 2,3).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results with reference to figures and supplementary files.

claim: Proteins from all three complement pathways were significantly anti-correlated with seroconversion including C1QA, C1QB, C1QC, C1R, and C1S (classical pathway); C2, C4A, and C4B (classical and lectin pathways); C3 (lectin and alternative pathways); and C6, C7, C8A, C8B, C8G, and C9 (terminal pathway).
source: Proteins from all three pathways were significantly anti-correlated with seroconversion including C1QA, C1QB, C1QC, C1R, and C1S, all involved in initiation of the classical pathway; C2, C4A, and C4B, which share functions in activation of the classical and lectin pathways; C3, which acts both in the lectin and alternative pathways; as well as C6, C7, C8A, C8B, C8G, and C9, which act in the downstream terminal pathway (Figure 4a).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results with reference to Figure 4a.

claim: Seroconversion correlates negatively with positive regulators of the complement cascade, such as GC, FCN3, CFB, and CFP.
source: Additionally, seroconversion correlates negatively with positive regulators of the complement cascade, such as GC (GC Vitamin D Binding Protein), which enhances the chemotactic activity of C5 alpha for neutrophils in inflammation and mediates macrophage activation (Kew et al., 1995); FCN3 (Ficolin 3), a protein involved in activation of the lectin complement pathway (Hein et al., 2010); CFB (Complement Factor B, C3/C5 Convertase); and CFP (Complement Factor P, Properdin).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results with citations to prior work describing protein functions.

claim: GC enhances the chemotactic activity of C5 alpha for neutrophils in inflammation and mediates macrophage activation.
source: Additionally, seroconversion correlates negatively with positive regulators of the complement cascade, such as GC (GC Vitamin D Binding Protein), which enhances the chemotactic activity of C5 alpha for neutrophils in inflammation and mediates macrophage activation (Kew et al., 1995); FCN3 (Ficolin 3), a protein involved in activation of the lectin complement pathway (Hein et al., 2010); CFB (Complement Factor B, C3/C5 Convertase); and CFP (Complement Factor P, Properdin).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Kew et al., 1995) describing GC function.

claim: FCN3 is a protein involved in activation of the lectin complement pathway.
source: Additionally, seroconversion correlates negatively with positive regulators of the complement cascade, such as GC (GC Vitamin D Binding Protein), which enhances the chemotactic activity of C5 alpha for neutrophils in inflammation and mediates macrophage activation (Kew et al., 1995); FCN3 (Ficolin 3), a protein involved in activation of the lectin complement pathway (Hein et al., 2010); CFB (Complement Factor B, C3/C5 Convertase); and CFP (Complement Factor P, Properdin).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Hein et al., 2010) describing FCN3 function.

claim: Most complement factors are significantly elevated in sero-low COVID19 patients relative to controls, but return to baseline or below baseline levels in sero-high patients.
source: Most of these factors are significantly elevated in sero-low COVID19 patients relative to controls, but return to baseline or below baseline levels in sero-high patients (Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured complement factor levels with reference to figures.

claim: Negative modulators of complement function showed similar behaviors, such as CFH, C4BPB, and SERPING1, suggesting the induction of negative feedback mechanisms during complement activation in sero-low patients.
source: Negative modulators of complement function showed similar behaviors, such as CFH (Complement Factor H), C4BPB (C4b binding protein), and SERPING1 (C1 inhibitor), suggesting the induction of negative feedback mechanisms during complement activation in sero-low patients (Figure 4a).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured complement regulator levels with interpretation and reference to Figure 4a.

claim: SOMAscan signals for C5 and the C5.C6 complex showed the opposite behavior, with lower signals in sero-low COVID19 patients, which could be interpreted as increased consumption of the C5 precursor polypeptide by the C5 convertase.
source: Only SOMAscan signals for C5 and the C5.C6 complex showed the opposite behavior, with lower signals in sero-low COVID19 patients, which could be interpreted as increased consumption of the C5 precursor polypeptide by the C5 convertase (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured C5 levels with speculative interpretation and reference to figures.

claim: Positive correlations with seroconversion indices were dominated by markers of platelet degranulation.
source: Among these factors, positive correlations with seroconversion indices were dominated by markers of platelet degranulation (Figure 5a), including key proteins stored in platelet alpha granules, such as SERPINA3 (alpha-1-antichymotrypsin, ACT), PDGFD (platelet derived growth factor D), SELP (selectin P), and GP1BA (glycoprotein Ib alpha) (Figure 5a–c, Supplementary file 9).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results with reference to figures and supplementary files.

claim: Key proteins stored in platelet alpha granules include SERPINA3, PDGFD, SELP, and GP1BA.
source: Among these factors, positive correlations with seroconversion indices were dominated by markers of platelet degranulation (Figure 5a), including key proteins stored in platelet alpha granules, such as SERPINA3 (alpha-1-antichymotrypsin, ACT), PDGFD (platelet derived growth factor D), SELP (selectin P), and GP1BA (glycoprotein Ib alpha) (Figure 5a–c, Supplementary file 9).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured protein levels with reference to figures and supplementary files.

claim: Except for SERPINA3, all platelet alpha granule factors are depleted in sero-low patients relative to the control cohort, and all four factors are significantly elevated in sero-high patients relative to sero-low patients.
source: Except for SERPINA3, all factors are depleted in sero-low patients relative to the control cohort, and all four factors are significantly elevated in sero-high patients relative to sero-low patients (Figure 5a,c).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured protein levels with reference to figures.

claim: Top negative correlations with seroconversion in both proteomics data sets include key modulators of the intrinsic and extrinsic coagulation pathways.
source: Conversely, top negative correlations with seroconversion in both proteomics data sets include key modulators of the intrinsic and extrinsic coagulation pathways.
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results.

claim: Many positive regulators of coagulation are elevated in sero-low patients and depleted in sero-high patients, including HABP2, SERPINF2, F7, F2, F11, F12, F10, FGA, and FGB.
source: Many positive regulators of coagulation are elevated in sero-low patients and depleted in sero-high patients, including HABP2 (hyaluronan activated binding protein 2, factor VII activating protein, FSAP), SERPINF2 (alpha-2-plasmin inhibitor), F7 (Coagulation Factor VII), F2 (Coagulation Factor II, thrombin), F11 (Coagulation Factor XI), F12 (Coagulation Factor XII), and F10 (Coagulation Factor X), as well as the structural components FGA (Fibrinogen Alpha Chain) and FGB (Fibrinogen Beta Chain) (Figure 5a,d,e, Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured coagulation factor levels with reference to figures.

claim: Many endogenous anticoagulants and drivers of fibrinolysis show a similar pattern, such as SERPINC1, SERPINA10, PLG, and PLAU.
source: However, many endogenous anticoagulants and drivers of fibrinolysis also show a similar pattern, such as SERPINC1 (antithrombin, AT-III), SERPINA10 (antitrypsin), PLG (Plasminogen), and PLAU (Plasminogen Activator, Urokinase).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured anticoagulant factor levels.

claim: SERPINC1 is a potent inhibitor of thrombin, as well as coagulation factors IXa, Xa, and XIa.
source: SERPINC1 is a potent inhibitor of thrombin, as well as coagulation factors IXa, Xa, and XIa (Rau et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Rau et al., 2007) describing SERPINC1 function.

claim: SERPIN10A is another inhibitor of coagulation factors Xa and XIa.
source: SERPIN10A is another inhibitor of coagulation factors Xa and XIa (Rau et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Rau et al., 2007) describing SERPIN10A function.

claim: Plasminogen is the precursor of plasmin, the key enzyme in fibrinolysis, and PLAU mediates proteolytic generation of plasmin.
source: Plasminogen is the precursor of plasmin, the key enzyme in fibrinolysis, and PLAU mediates proteolytic generation of plasmin.
evidence: The manuscript describes established knowledge about plasminogen and PLAU function.

claim: Several kallikreins, including KLKB1, KLK12, KLK10, and KLK12, as well as KNG1 (kininogen) are all depleted in seroconverted patients.
source: Lastly, several kallikreins, including KLKB1, KLK12, KLK10, and KLK12, as well as KNG1 (kininogen) are all depleted in seroconverted patients (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured kallikrein and kininogen levels with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: The kinin-kallikrein system plays key roles in coagulation, inflammation, and blood pressure control.
source: The kinin-kallikrein system plays key roles in coagulation, inflammation, and blood pressure control (Wu, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Wu, 2015) describing kinin-kallikrein system function.

claim: Once activated, kallikreins function as serine proteases that can cleave plasminogen into plasmin, thus promoting fibrinolysis, but also high-molecular weight kininogen (HMWK) into the vasoactive peptide bradykinin, thus promoting vasodilation.
source: Once activated, kallikreins function as serine proteases that can cleave plasminogen into plasmin, thus promoting fibrinolysis, but also high-molecular weight kininogen (HMWK) into the vasoactive peptide bradykinin, thus promoting vasodilation (Wu, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work (Wu, 2015) describing kallikrein function.

claim: Both platelet counts and D-dimer correlated positively with the seroconversion scores.
source: Both platelet counts and D-dimer correlated positively with the seroconversion scores (Figure 5f).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results with reference to Figure 5f.

claim: Platelet counts were significantly lower in the sero-low group relative to the sero-high group, with ~30% of sero-low patients being considered thrombocytopenic.
source: Platelet counts were significantly lower in the sero-low group relative to the sero-high group, with ~30% of sero-low patients being considered thrombocytopenic (Figure 5g, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured platelet counts with reference to figures and supplementary files.

claim: D-dimer levels were significantly higher in the sero-high group relative to the sero-low group, with the mean value for this group being well above the accepted threshold of 500 ng/mL.
source: D-dimer levels were significantly higher in the sero-high group relative to the sero-low group, with the mean value for this group being well above the accepted threshold of 500 ng/mL (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured D-dimer levels with reference to supplementary file.

claim: Very few measurements of D-dimer were available for the control group, which were highly variable and not significantly different from the sero-low group.
source: Very few measurements of D-dimer were available for the control group, which were highly variable and not significantly different from the sero-low group (Figure 5g).
evidence: The manuscript reports measured D-dimer levels with reference to Figure 5g.

claim: Seroconversion correlated positively and significantly with absolute neutrophil count (ANC), WBC count, and absolute lymphocyte count (ALC).
source: In addition to the aforementioned positive correlations with platelet counts and D-dimer levels, seroconversion correlated positively and significantly with absolute neutrophil count (ANC), WBC count, and absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) (Figure 6a–c, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a, Supplementary file 10).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results with reference to figures and supplementary files.

claim: ANC, WBC count, and ALC are lower in the sero-low COVID19 patients, with mean values toward the low end of normal ranges, but increase significantly in sero-high patients.
